title: ABCD SYNDROME
alt_titles: ALBINISM, BLACK LOCK, CELL MIGRATION DISORDER OF THE NEUROCYTES OF THE GUT, AND DEAFNESS

intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the endothelin receptor type B gene (EDNRB; 131244) on chromosome 13q22.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome (ABCDS) is caused by homozygous mutation in the endothelin receptor type B gene (EDNRB).
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is caused by a homozygous mutation in the EDNRB gene.

checks.claim: The EDNRB gene is located on chromosome 13q22.
checks.evidence_quote: we screened DNA of the index patient of the ABCD syndrome family for mutations in the endothelin B receptor (EDNRB) gene
checks.explanation: The abstract does not give the 13q22 location. Under the rules, adding a gene's standard chromosomal location counts as standard nomenclature that restates the paper.

paragraphs.text: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive neurocristopathy. Its name is an acronym for its cardinal features: albinism, a black lock of hair, a cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease, or intestinal aganglionosis), and sensorineural deafness. The disorder is now thought to belong to the Waardenburg-Shah (Waardenburg syndrome type 4) spectrum caused by EDNRB mutations.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder.
checks.evidence_quote: ABCD syndrome is an autosomal recessive syndrome characterized by albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease [HSCR]), and deafness.
It represents a new neural crest syndrome with autosomal-recessive inheritance.
checks.explanation: The abstract calls it a neural crest syndrome, which means a neurocristopathy.

checks.claim: The name ABCD syndrome is an acronym for its cardinal features: albinism, a black lock of hair, a cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut (Hirschsprung disease or intestinal aganglionosis), and sensorineural deafness.
checks.evidence_quote: Autosomal-recessive neural crest syndrome with albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and deafness: ABCD syndrome.
checks.explanation: The title gives the acronym and its four parts. The abstract says only 'deafness' (bilateral, confirmed by BAEP); it does not specify 'sensorineural' and does not use the term Hirschsprung disease.

checks.claim: ABCD syndrome is now thought to belong to the Waardenburg-Shah syndrome (Waardenburg syndrome type 4) spectrum caused by EDNRB mutations.
checks.evidence_quote: We therefore suggest that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity, but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.
checks.explanation: Shah-Waardenburg syndrome is the same disorder as Waardenburg syndrome type 4. The abstract also says EDNRB is involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.

paragraphs.text: Gross et al. (1995) described the syndrome in a child of Kurdish origin. The child had albinism of the skin and hair except for a black lock of hair, intestinal aganglionosis (Hirschsprung disease), and deafness. Gross et al. (1995) regarded these features as a newly recognized disorder of neural crest cell migration and named it with the acronym ABCD.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) described ABCD syndrome in a child of Kurdish origin.
checks.evidence_quote: She was the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents.

checks.claim: The Kurdish child with ABCD syndrome described by Gross et al. (1995) had albinism of the skin and hair, except for a black lock of hair.
checks.evidence_quote: We report on a macrosomic newborn girl with albinism, a black lock at the right temporo-occipital region, and retinal depigmentation.
checks.explanation: The abstract reports albinism and a black lock, but it does not say the albinism affected 'the skin and hair' or that the lock was the only pigmented hair.

checks.claim: The Kurdish child with ABCD syndrome described by Gross et al. (1995) had intestinal aganglionosis (Hirschsprung disease).
checks.evidence_quote: Biopsy showed aganglionosis of the large intestine, and total absence of neurocytes and nerve fibers in the small intestine

checks.claim: The Kurdish child with ABCD syndrome described by Gross et al. (1995) was deaf.
checks.evidence_quote: Bilateral deafness was confirmed by brainstem auditory-evoked potentials.
checks.explanation: The abstract states the patient was deaf.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) regarded the combination of albinism, a black lock of hair, intestinal aganglionosis and deafness as a newly recognized disorder of neural crest cell migration.
checks.evidence_quote: A syndrome of albinism, black lock, deafness, and a total lack of intestinal neural innervation has not yet been reported. It represents a new neural crest syndrome
checks.explanation: The authors regarded the combination as a new neural crest disorder, and the title describes a cell migration disorder.

checks.claim: Gross et al. (1995) named the disorder with the acronym ABCD.
checks.evidence_quote: albinism, black lock, cell migration disorder of the neurocytes of the gut, and deafness: ABCD syndrome.
checks.explanation: The title names the disorder ABCD syndrome.

paragraphs.text: The family reported by Gross et al. (1995) suggested autosomal recessive inheritance. Verheij et al. (2002) confirmed this pattern when they found a homozygous EDNRB mutation in the original patient.

checks.claim: The family with ABCD syndrome reported by Gross et al. (1995) suggested autosomal recessive inheritance.
checks.evidence_quote: She was the 14th child of consanguineous Kurdish parents. Four sibs of our patient had the same syndrome and died a few days after birth.
checks.explanation: The family had consanguineous parents and several affected sibs, and the authors concluded autosomal recessive inheritance.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) confirmed autosomal recessive inheritance of ABCD syndrome by finding a homozygous EDNRB mutation in the original patient reported by Gross et al. (1995).
checks.evidence_quote: we screened DNA of the index patient of the ABCD syndrome family for mutations in the endothelin B receptor (EDNRB) gene, a gene known to be involved in Shah-Waardenburg syndrome. A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: The abstract confirms a homozygous mutation in the index patient of a syndrome it calls autosomal recessive. It does not mention Gross et al. (1995) or say the patient is the one they originally reported; that link is not in the abstract.

paragraphs.text: In the patient originally reported by Gross et al. (1995), Verheij et al. (2002) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation in the EDNRB gene (arg201-to-ter; R201X). They concluded that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but part of the spectrum of Waardenburg syndrome type 4 (Shah-Waardenburg syndrome) caused by EDNRB mutation.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) identified a homozygous nonsense mutation, arg201-to-ter (R201X), in the EDNRB gene in the ABCD syndrome patient originally reported by Gross et al. (1995).
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: The homozygous R201X nonsense mutation is confirmed. The abstract refers only to the 'index patient of the ABCD syndrome family'; it does not say this is the patient Gross et al. (1995) reported.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) concluded that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity but part of the spectrum of Waardenburg syndrome type 4 (Shah-Waardenburg syndrome) caused by EDNRB mutation.
checks.evidence_quote: We therefore suggest that ABCD syndrome is not a separate entity, but an expression of Shah-Waardenburg syndrome.
checks.explanation: The abstract states this conclusion directly.

paragraphs.text: In the patient with ABCD syndrome originally reported by Gross et al. (1995), Verheij et al. (2002) identified a homozygous arg201-to-ter (R201X) nonsense mutation in the EDNRB gene.

checks.claim: Verheij et al. (2002) identified a homozygous arg201-to-ter (R201X) nonsense mutation in the EDNRB gene in the ABCD syndrome patient originally reported by Gross et al. (1995).
checks.evidence_quote: A homozygous nonsense mutation in exon 3 (R201X) of the EDNRB gene was found.
checks.explanation: The homozygous R201X mutation is confirmed. The abstract does not mention Gross et al. (1995) and does not say this is their original patient.
